'''will-o’-the-wisp''' (wil′ọ-thē̤-wisp), ''n.'' '''1.''' The ignis fatuus; hence, any person or thing that deludes or misleads by dazzling, visionary, or evanescent appearances. Also ''will-in-the-wisp'', ''will-with-a-wisp'', and ''Jack o’ lantern.''
{{smaller block|All this hide and seek, this ''will-in-the-wisp'', has no other meaning than a Christian marriage for sweet Mrs. Belinda.
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Provoked Wife, v. 3.}}
<poem>
Wicked sea-''will-o’-the-wisp!''
Wolf of the shore! dog, with thy lying lights
Thou hast betray’d us on these rocks of thine!
</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Harold, ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' A common fresh-water alga, ''Nostoc commune:'' so named from its sudden and seemingly mysterious appearance. See ''Nostoc.''

'''willow'''<sup>1</sup> (wil′ō), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [Also dial. ''willy''; < ME. ''wilowe'', ''wylow'', ''weloghe'', ''wilwe'', ''wilze'', < AS. ''welig'' = MD. ''welighe'', ''wilghe'', later ''wilge'', D. ''wilg'' = MLG. LG. ''wilge'', willow; root uncertain. For other names, cf. ''sallow''<sup>2</sup> and ''withy''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' {{RunningHeader|will|6928|'''willow'''}}{{nop}}{{smaller block|The one to be ''willed'' would go to the other end of the house, if desired, whilst we agreed upon the thing to be done. {{right|''Proc. Soc. Psych. Research'', I. 57, note.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To wish; desire; prefer; resolve; determine; decree. {{smaller block|As ''will'' the rest, so ''willeth'' Winchester. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 162.}}}} {{smaller block|You, likewise, our late guests, if so you ''will'', Follow us. {{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, v.}}}} '''2.''' To exercise the will. {{smaller block|See how my sin-bemangled body lies, Not having pow’r to ''will'', nor will to rise! {{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, iv. 8.}}}} {{smaller block|He that shall turn his thoughts inwards upon what passes in his own mind when he ''wills'', shall see that the will or power of volition is conversant about nothing but that particular determination of the mind, whereby barely, by a thought, the mind endeavours to give rise, continuation, or stop to any action which it takes to be within its power. {{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, II. xxi. § 30.}}}} '''will3†''', ''a.''   [Sc. also ''wull''; < ME. ''will'', ''wille'', < Icel. ''villr'' (for *''vildr''), wild: see ''wild''.]   Astray; wrong; at a loss; bewildered. {{smaller block|Adam went out ful ''wille'' o wan. {{right|Quoted in ''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), Gloss., p. 213.}}}} {{smaller block|All wery I wex and ''wyll'' of my gate. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2369.}}}} {{smaller block|And ''wull'' and waif for eight lang years They sail’d upon the sea. {{right|''Rosmer Hafmand'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 253).}}}} '''will3†''', ''v. i.''   [< ''will''3, ''a.'']   To wander; go astray; be lost, at a loss, or bewildered. ''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2359. '''willcock''' (wil′kok), ''n.'' Same as ''willock''. '''willed''' (wild), ''a.''   [< ME. ''willed''; < ''will''1, ''n.'', + ''-ed''2.]   '''1.''' Having a will; determined as to will: usually in composition, as in self-''willed'', weak-''willed''. {{smaller block|He is ''wylled'' that comynycasyon and trete schold be had. {{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 75.}}}} '''2.''' Brought under the influence or control of the will of another. '''willemite''' (wil′em-īt), ''n.''   [Named after ''Willem'' I., king of the Netherlands.]   A mineral of resinous luster and yellowish-green or flesh-red color, a native silicate of zinc. {{smaller|It is of rare occurrence in Europe, but is found abundantly in New Jersey, and there constitutes a very valuable zinc ore. Troostite is a crystallized variety containing some manganese.}} '''willer''' (wil′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''will''1 + ''-er''1.]   '''1.''' One who wishes; a wisher: used in some rare compounds: as, an ill-''willer''.—'''2.''' One who wills. {{smaller block|Be pleased to cast a glance on two considerations—1. What the will is to which, 2. Who the ''willer'' is to whom, we must submit. {{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, II. xxxvi.}}}} {{smaller block|The problem can never be solved as long as contact of any sort is allowed between the ''willer'' and the willed. {{right|''Proc. Soc. Psych. Research'', II. 10.}}}} '''willet''' (wil′et), ''n.''   [So called from its cry; cf. ''pill-will-willet''.]   A North American bird of the snipe family, the semipalmated tattler or stone-curlew, ''Symphemia semipalmata''. {{smaller|It is a large, stout tattler with semipalmated toes (see cut under ''semipalmate''), stout bill, bluish feet, and muchvariegated plumage, especially in summer, the wings being mirrored with white and lined with black; the length is about 16 inches. It abounds in temperate North America, and especially in the United States; it extends north to 56° at least, breeds throughout its range, and winters in the Southern States. Some related tattlers are occasionally mistaken for the species, and called ''willet'' by sportsmen. See ''Symphemia.''}} {{smaller block|Across the dune, curlews, gulls, pelicans, water-turkeys, and ''willets'' were feeding. {{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXX. 223.}}}} [[File:century v08 p0732 c1f1.png|center|244px]] {{c|{{smaller|Willet (''Symphemia semipalmata''), in winter plumage.}}}} '''willful, willfully,''' etc. See ''wilful'', etc. '''willick,''' ''n.'' A Scotch variant of ''willock''. '''willie,''' ''a.'' Same as ''willy''1. '''willie-fisher''' (wil′i-fish″ėr), ''n.'' The common tern or sea-swallow. See cut under ''Sterna''. [Forfar, Scotland.] '''willie-hawkie''' (wil′i-hâ′ki), ''n.'' The little grebe, or dabchick.   ''C. Swainson.'' [Antrim, Ireland.] '''willie-man-beard''' (wil′i-man-bērd′), ''n.'' The sea-stickleback, ''Spinachia vulgaris.'' Compare cut under ''stickleback.'' [Local, Eng.] '''willie-muftie''', ''n.'' See ''willy-mufty.'' '''williewaught''' (wil′i-wâċht), ''n.''   [< ''willie'' (here used with dim. effect) + ''waught.'']   A hearty draught of liquor. [Scotch.] An’ we’ll tak’ a right guid ''willie-waught'' For auld lang syne.   ''Burns,'' Auld Lang Syne. '''willing''' (wil′ing), ''n.''   [< ME. ''willing''; verbal n. of ''will''1, ''v.'']   Inclination; desire; intention. {{smaller block|The evil natures, and the evil principles, and the evil manners of the world, these are the causes of our imperfect ''willings'' and weaker actings in the things of God. {{right|''Jer. Taylor,'' Works (ed. 1835), II. 13.}}}} '''willing''' (wil′ing), ''a.''   [< ME. ''willing'', for earlier ''willende'', < AS. ''willende'', ''wellende'', ppr. of ''willan'', will: see ''will''1. ''Willing'' in mod. use also represents the ppr. of ''will''2.]   '''1.''' Favorably disposed; ready; inclined; desirous: as, ''willing'' to work; ''willing'' to depart. {{smaller block|I shall be ''willing'', if not apt, to learn. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.,'' Philaster, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|King Henry, having entred a Throne in a Storm, was ''willing'' now to have a Calm. {{right|''Baker,'' Chronicles, p. 157.}}}} {{smaller block|If others make easier conditions of blessedness, no wonder if their doctrine be entertained by those who are ''willing'' to be happy but unwilling to leave their sins. {{right|''Stillingfleet,'' Sermons, II. ii.}}}} {{smaller block|I never hear any thing of the Countess [of Oxford] except just now, that she is grown tired of sublunary affairs, and ''willing'' to come to a composition with her lord. {{right|''Walpole,'' Letters, II. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|The 21st day Captain Eaton came to an Anchor by us; he was very ''willing'' to have consorted with us again. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 133.}}}} '''2.''' Voluntary; cheerfully given, granted, done, or borne: as, ''willing'' service; ''willing'' poverty. {{smaller block|I raise him thus, and with this ''willing'' kiss I seal his pardon. {{right|''Fletcher (and another ?)'', Prophetess, iv. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Sad Ulysses’ soul, and all the rest, Are held with his melodious harmony In ''willing'' chains and sweet captivity. {{right|''Milton'', Vacation Exercise, l. 52.}}}} {{smaller block|The chief is apt to get an extra share [of the spoils], either by actual capture, or by the ''willing'' award of his comrades. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 542.}}}} '''3.''' Characterized by promptness or readiness in action; free from reluctance, laziness, or slowness: as, a ''willing'' horse; a ''willing'' hand. {{smaller block|Mount the decks, and call the ''willing'' wind. {{right|''Pope'', Odyssey, ix. 655.}}}} '''4†.''' In harmony or accord; like-minded. {{smaller block|I am perswaded the Devill himselfe was never ''willing'' with their proceedings. {{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 22.}}}} {{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Minded.—'''2.''' ''Spontaneous'', etc. See ''voluntary''.}} '''willing-hearted''' (wil′ing-här″ted), ''a.'' Well-inclined; heartily consenting. Ex. xxxv. 22. '''willingly''' (wil′ing-li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''willingly''; < ''willing'' + ''-ly''2.]   In a willing manner. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Of one’s own will, choice, or consent; voluntarily; knowingly.}} {{smaller block|Heer I swere that never ''willingly'' In werk ne thought I nil yow disobeye. {{right|''Chaucer'', Clerk’s Tale, l. 306.}}}} {{smaller block|By labour and intense study, . . . joined with the strong propensity of nature, I might perhaps leave something so written to after-times as they should not ''willingly'' let it die. {{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, ii., Int.}}}} (''b'') Readily; cheerfully. {{smaller block|Not . . . as it were of necessity, but ''willingly.'' {{right|Phile. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|Proud of employment, ''willingly'' I go. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., ii. 1. 35.}}}} {{smaller block|They would ''willingly'' haue beene friends, or haue giuen any composition they could. {{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 90.}}}} '''willingness''' (wil′ing-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state or character of being willing; free choice or consent of the will; readiness. {{smaller block|I would expend it with all ''willingness.'' {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 150.}}}} {{smaller block|Satan o’ercomes none but by ''Willingnesse.'' {{right|''Herrick'', Temptations.}}}} {{smaller block|Many brauado’s they made, but, to appease their fury, our Captaine prepared with as seeming a ''willingnesse'' (as they) to incounter them. {{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 177.}}}} {{smaller block|Sweet is the love which comes with ''willingness.'' {{right|''Dryden'', Aurengzebe, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|They one after another declared their conviction of their errors, and their ''willingness'' to receive baptism. {{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 6.}}}} '''2†.''' Good will; readiness. {{smaller block|We, having now the best at Barnet field, Will thither straight, for ''willingness'' rids way. {{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., v. 3. 21.}}}} ='''Syn. 1.''' ''Forwardness, Willingness.'' See ''forwardness.'' '''will-in-the-wisp''' (wil′in-thē̤-wisp), ''n.'' Same as ''will-o’-the-wisp.'' '''Willisian''' (wil′is-i-a̤n), ''a.''   [< ''Willis'' (see def.) + ''-ian.'']   Of or pertaining to Thomas Willis, an English anatomist, famous for his researches on the brain and nerves. {{smaller|Specifically, in ''anat.'': (''a'') Noting a remarkable anastomosis of arteries at the base of the brain. See ''circle of Willis'', under ''circle''. (''b'') Noting the old enumeration of nine pairs of cranial nerves (now counted as twelve pairs).}} '''Willis’s disease.''' Diabetes. '''williwaw''' (wil′i-wâ), ''n.''   [Origin obscure.]   A sudden, violent squall of wind. Also spelled ''willywaw.'' {{smaller block|Those whirlwind squalls, formerly called, by the sealers in Tierra del Fuego, ''williwaws''. They may be truly termed hurricane squalls—like those at Gibraltar, in a violent Levanter. {{right|''Fitz Roy'', Weather Book, p. 125.}}}} '''will-less''' (wil′les), ''a.''   [< ''will''1 + ''-less.'']   '''1.''' Lacking will-power; having no will or volition; not volitional. {{smaller block|A merely knowing, quite ''will-less'' being. {{right|''Du Prel'', Philos. of Mysticism (trans. 1889), II. 8.}}}} '''2.''' Involuntary. {{smaller block|Your blind duty and ''will-less'' resignation. {{right|''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, I. xv.}}}} '''willock''' (wil′o̤k), ''n.''   [Cf. Sc. ''willick'', a young heron, also the puffin.]   The common murre or guillemot, ''Uria troile'' or ''Lomvia troile'', a bird of the auk family, abundant on both coasts of the North Atlantic.
